summary: Full-extraction pass over seven IMF Article IV staff reports on St. Lucia (2017-2025), eight Estimates of Revenue and Expenditure (2016-17 to 2024-25, without 2023-24) and the National Economic Fund Act 2019. Adds the remaining columns of the IMF CIP revenue lines (EC$ million and % of GDP; image tables in 2022 and 2023 OCR'd), the 2017 IMF box on the programme's first year and rule changes, every column of the CIP revenue, CIU-surplus and NEF lines in the Estimates (including printed zeros and forward estimates), the CIP capital project 274, CIP revenue as a capital-financing source, individual zero-interest CIP bonds in the 2017-18 to 2019-20 debt schedules (investor names left out) and one NEF-financed project.

events.title: National Economic Fund Act passed by Parliament
events.description: Saint Lucia National Economic Fund Act No. 18 of 2019 passed by the House of Assembly on 11 June 2019 and the Senate on 13 June 2019. It replaces section 33 of the CBI Act: CBI cash contributions ("qualifying investments") go to the Fund, run by a board chaired by the Director of Finance, which may lend to or invest in government-approved capital projects, reduce government debt, buy government bonds or fund non-recurrent purposes approved by Cabinet, and must publish an annual report.
events.quote: Passed in the Senate this 13th day of June, 2019.

events.title: National Economic Fund Act in force
events.description: Commencement date printed in the Act: from this date the Saint Lucia National Economic Fund under Act No. 18 of 2019 receives CBI cash contributions, and references in the CBI Act to the Fund refer to it (s. 20).

gaps: The Estimates list CIP bonds individually only in 2017-18 to 2019-20; later volumes show no CIP or COVID-19 relief bonds in the debt schedule, so bond holdings after 2019 cannot be traced in these documents.

ledger.contains: IMF 2017 Article IV staff report on St. Lucia (75 pp.). CIP content: Box 3 (p. 18) on the programme's first year (6 real estate approvals, 14 donation applications for US$1.4 million, 5 bond approvals for US$2.7 million), the 2016/17 rule changes (donation cut from US$200,000 to US$100,000, US$50,000 bond admin fee, 500 cap and US$3 million affidavit removed, US$300,000 real estate and US$1 million enterprise minimums) and the authorities' 2017/18 expectations (US$9 million donations, 80% to government, 36 real estate applications); Table 2a/2b (pp. 32-33) CIP revenue line 2013-2022 in EC$ million and % of GDP; paras 18 and 37 (risks, sovereign wealth fund plan, no numbers). The 80% transfer rule is already in events from the 2017 regulations and is not added again; the rule changes of January 2017 are already events. Rest of the report (macro, banking, debt sustainability) is out of scope.

IMF 2018 Article IV staff report (86 pp.). CIP content: Table 2a/2b (pp. 29-30) CIP revenue line 2014-2023 in EC$ million and % of GDP (2017 budget column included); staff adjustment-scenario text table (p. 14) with CIP as a financing source of a proposed natural disasters fund 2018-2021 (% of GDP); paras on reputational risk, due diligence and a planned residency programme (no numbers). Rest (macro, fiscal, banking, DSA, AML/CFT) out of scope.

IMF 2019 Article IV staff report (82 pp., published Feb 2020). CIP content: Table 2a/2b (pp. 31-32) CIP revenue 2015-2024 in EC$ million and % of GDP; para 6 (p. 10) repeats the 1.3% of GDP for 2018 shown in Table 2b (already recorded) and says applications declined sharply in 2019 (no count); plans for a National Economic Fund and a self-insurance fund financed by CIP revenue (no amounts); chart on p. 26 with no printed CIP values. Rest out of scope.

IMF 2022 Article IV staff report (67 pp.); statistical tables are images (OCR used). CIP content: Table 2a/2b (pp. 32-33, images) CIP revenue 2018-2027 in EC$ million and % of GDP with footnote 3/ on what the line covers; footnote 17 (p. 17) on the bond option and ~1% of GDP fresh financing in FY2021 (already recorded); risk and AML/CFT paragraphs (EU scrutiny, tax-evasion checks not done) with no numbers. BoP, monetary and other tables (pp. 31, 34-37) have no CIP line. Rest out of scope.

IMF 2023 Article IV staff report (65 pp., published March 2024); statistical tables are images (OCR used). CIP content: Table 2a/2b (pp. 32-33, images) CIP revenue 2019-2028 in EC$ million and % of GDP; paras 5, 12, 23, 25 (CIP revenue growth in FY2022, risk, advice to save CIP proceeds; a sinking fund for revenue from the bond option, used only for debt service, with no amount or date); risk matrix (EU pressure). BoP and monetary tables (pp. 34-35) have no CIP line. Rest out of scope.

IMF 2024 Article IV staff report (74 pp., published March 2025). CIP content: Table 2 (p. 28) CIP revenue 2020-2029 in % of GDP (no EC$ table); paras 19 and 39 with footnotes 17-18 (due diligence tightened under the 2023 US-Caribbean roundtable; real estate/enterprise project data not available; transfers via the National Economic Fund should be simplified) and the data annex (CIP Unit shares no escrow or land-sale data): no numbers. Rest out of scope.

IMF 2025 Article IV staff report (74 pp., published January 2026). CIP content: Table 2 (p. 33) CIP revenue 2020-2030 in % of GDP; paras 7, 20, 44 and Annex (CIP supported revenue in FY2024/25; cabinet recently approved a first sovereign wealth fund financed by CIP proceeds, no date or amount; regional regulator; due diligence strengthened); data annex (CIP Unit shares no escrow data). No other CIP numbers. Rest out of scope.

The Covid-19 emergency response is financed by 'BONDS' without saying whether CIP bonds: not recorded. Everything else out of scope.

Saint Lucia 2024-25 Estimates of Revenue & Expenditure (768 pp.). CIP content: National Economic Fund line among grants in the Summary of Government Operations (p. 8: EC$2,661,825 actual 2022-23, zero after); item 004 'Surplus Revenue From CIP' all zero 2022/23-2026/27 (p. 55). No 'Citizenship by Investment fee' or NEF contribution revenue items, no NEF-financed project. Ordinary citizenship fees (item 083) and other lines out of scope.

Saint Lucia National Economic Fund Act No. 18 of 2019 (8 pp.): establishes the NEF funded by CBI cash contributions (s. 36(4)(b) CBI Act), its functions (loans and investment in government-approved capital projects, debt reduction, bond purchases, non-recurrent Cabinet-approved purposes), a board of 5-7 members chaired by the Director of Finance, April-March financial year, audit, annual report (applications, amounts), repeal of s. 33 of the CBI Act. No programme amounts or fees. Assent (2 July 2019) was already an event; passage (13 June) and commencement (3 July) added.
